extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, filmmakers, and storytellers (creative-writing practitioners focused on film and dramatic narrative)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and writing film stories: placing a work on the Archplot–Miniplot–Antiplot spectrum, building setting and structure, avoiding cliché, and doing the research and craft work necessary to make a story original and producible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story design triangle: Archplot / Miniplot / Antiplot / Nonplot
rubrics_metrics.description: Place your story somewhere on the story design triangle: classical Archplot (closed, active, causal), Miniplot (internalized, passive, open), Antiplot (inconsistent realities, fractured causality), or Nonplot (stasis, portraiture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each side is a spectrum of structural choices; most works blend elements and slide along these lines rather than sit at an extreme. Examples: CHINATOWN and THE SEVEN SAMURAI (Archplot); FIVE EASY PIECES (Miniplot); BARTON FINK (mixed, central); MONTY PYTHON (Antiplot/absurd). Understand the qualities of each form before choosing or blending them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change versus Stasis (story arc requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether your story will enact clear change (arc) or remain in stasis (Nonplot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Above the Miniplot/Antiplot dividing line life clearly changes (even if subtly). Below it stories remain in stasis and do not arc; they become portraiture or absurd satire. Use this to determine whether your story will deliver an arc for the character(s) or a static portrait. Examples: HUSBANDS (change), UMBERTO D / FACES (stasis/Nonplot).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for audience and commercial viability
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that as story design moves away from the Archplot toward Miniplot, Antiplot, and Nonplot, the audience generally shrinks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smaller audience implies smaller budgets and different production models. If writing for Hollywood (large budgets, mass audience) lean toward Archplot or ensure your nonclassical design has a realistic path to recoupment; if you accept a small budget and niche audience you can pursue Miniplot/Antiplot. Examples and discussion: Hollywood vs 'art film', Robbe-Grillet’s low-budget strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master the Classical (Archplot) form first
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn and be able to write classical Archplot design before attempting Miniplot or Antiplot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Miniplot and Antiplot are reactions to the Classical; to reduce or shatter the Classical form creatively you must understand it intimately. Examples: Bergman, Fellini, Godard, Altman started in classical forms before experimenting. Skill becomes craft when it moves from intellect to instinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writer must believe in what he writes (sincerity of vision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tale must reflect a passionate conviction about life—'I believe life is like this.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you don't truly believe the worldview your form implies (e.g., minimalism, anticlassicism), the work will smell phony. Avoid writing nonclassical forms merely to reject Hollywood; difference for the sake of difference is an empty political gesture, not creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: War on cliché: know your story’s world
rubrics_metrics.description: Cliché arises when a writer does not know the world of his story and resorts to copying scenes, dialogue, and characters from other works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originality derives from in-depth understanding of setting and its particulars. If you lack specific knowledge you will reheat literary leftovers. To avoid cliché, deeply learn the world (see Research metrics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting — Period
rubrics_metrics.description: PERIOD is a story's place in time (contemporary, historical, hypothetical future, or timeless/fantasy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide and fix the story's time period because it shapes character behavior, social context, and plot possibilities. This is one of the four dimensions that define a setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting — Duration
rubrics_metrics.description: DURATION is the story's span through time (seconds, minutes, hours, days, months, years, decades or rare cases where storytime equals screentime).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be deliberate about how much life your story covers; techniques like cross-cutting, overlap, repetition, and slow motion can expand screentime beyond storytime (Odessa Steps example). Duration affects pacing, scope, and the kinds of events you can credibly include.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting — Location
rubrics_metrics.description: LOCATION is the story's place in space — its specific geography, town, streets, buildings, rooms, landscapes, or planets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specificity matters: there is no 'America' generic setting. The particular neighborhood, city, or landscape will dictate which events are possible and what details are germane to credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting — Level of Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: LEVEL OF CONFLICT is the story's pitch on the hierarchy of human struggles (inner/unconscious, personal, institutional/social, environmental).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide at which level(s) the story operates. A setting includes its social/political/economic forces; the chosen level of conflict shapes character cast and plausible actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Creative Limitation: create a small, knowable world
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit your fictional universe so that the writer can know it in depth; 'small' means knowable, not trivial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A limited world allows commanding knowledge and richer creative choices, enabling original detail and avoiding dilution of insight. Examples: CRIME AND PUNISHMENT (microscopic focus), DR. STRANGELOVE (three sets, eight characters). The smaller the world the greater the potential for originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: A story must obey its own internal laws of probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you establish the causal principles and 'laws' of your fictional world, you must not break them; events must be possible or probable within that world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The audience inspects your universe from the first image and rejects works that violate their formed expectations of how things work. Fantasy can leap from reality once, but then requires tight probability; other genres may allow different 'laws' (e.g., USUAL SUSPECTS' law of free association).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commanding knowledge of 'what's germane' in your setting
rubrics_metrics.description: By the final draft the writer must possess a commanding knowledge of all details germane to the story (not every crevice of existence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This means you can instantly answer relevant questions about time, place, character habits, weather, customs, etc. It arises from focused research and living inside the small world you create.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research: memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Research of memory — recall and re-experience relevant personal memories that resonate with your character's situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vivid recall (e.g., a childhood fear) to infuse scenes with authentic feeling. Memory research turns private experience into working material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research: imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Research of imagination — simulate living your character’s life hour by hour to invent everyday details and plausible behaviors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch vivid routines, habits, rituals that may not appear in the script but build a lived-in world. Imagination stitches fragments into coherent, believable life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research: fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Research of fact — do library and factual research to expand knowledge beyond personal experience and cure blocks of ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factual research confirms the universality of your observations and deepens your material. Reading authoritative work on your subject will broaden insight (e.g., family dynamics for domestic drama) and often triggers creative breakthroughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: To use Miniplot/Antiplot effectively, play against Classical expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Miniplot and Antiplot require the writer to 'play with or against' the audience’s Classical expectations to make nonclassical design acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because audiences enter with Classical anticipation, you must carefully and creatively shatter or bend that form so the audience will accept inner life (Miniplot) or absurdity/inconsistent reality (Antiplot). Without grounding in Classical form this subversion will feel accidental or pretentious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage consistency of reality to avoid alienating the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful that inconsistent realities, mockumentary inserts, or false-realities inside a conventional narrative can push a work toward Antiplot and risk alienating viewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you intentionally use inconsistent realities (e.g., WHEN HARRY MET SALLY's faux-documentary interviews), do so knowingly and craft them to serve the story; accidental or unearned inconsistency will feel tedious or meaningless to most audiences.
